titre: A lawyer appointed on the morning of the trial
accroche: Alabama, 1931: seven young Black men are sentenced to death for rape without a real defender. In 1932, the Supreme Court explains why that is not enough.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 25, 1931, on a freight train crossing Alabama, a fight breaks out between young Black men and young white men. Two young white women on the train accuse Black men of having raped them. A sheriff's posse arrests nine of them before the Scottsboro station. The indictment is drawn up on March 31, and the trials begin on April 6, six days later.

## All the lawyers, therefore none

The record does not say who defends the accused. The court records do mention representation at the arraignment, but no one had been retained. On the morning of the first trial, April 6, no one answers for the accused. The judge explains that he had "appointed all the members of the bar" for the arraignment, counting on some of them to keep helping afterward. A Tennessee lawyer, who does not belong to the local bar, says he was spoken to about the case without having been retained and that he would like to help. A local lawyer agrees to assist him. The Supreme Court will sum it up drily: this is how, in a casual fashion, the question of counsel was settled in a capital case.

Each of the three trials is wrapped up in a single day. The juries impose the death penalty on all those convicted. Seven of them, whose convictions the Alabama Supreme Court has upheld, take the case to Washington. They are young, illiterate, strangers to the State, guarded by troops in a climate the Court finds hostile.

## A deliberately narrow rule

In *Powell v. Alabama*, argued on October 10 and decided on November 7, 1932, the U.S. Supreme Court overturns the convictions. It cannot contradict the Alabama Supreme Court on State law: Alabama's 1901 Constitution and a 1923 statute already required that counsel be appointed in a capital case. The problem was not the absence of a rule. It was the timing: an appointment made on the morning of the trial, when the most critical period, the time of preparation, had passed without any real help.

Justice Sutherland then ties this right to the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. A layman, he writes, does not know the rules of evidence and may be convicted on inadmissible evidence. But the formula adopted is narrow: in a capital case, when the accused cannot pay for a lawyer and is unable to defend himself because of ignorance, illiteracy or a similar cause, the court must appoint counsel even without a request, and early enough for it to be of any use. As for other cases, the Court says explicitly that it does not have to decide them.

## Thirty-one years of restraint

This caution has a cost. In 1942, in *Betts v. Brady*, a divided Court refuses to extend the requirement to the States for every criminal case. Only in 1963, in *Gideon v. Wainwright*, is that decision overturned: for serious crimes (felonies) tried by the States, a court-appointed lawyer becomes a right. *Powell* was only a first step, and one may wonder why it took so long to reach the second.

citation.texte: in a capital case, where the defendant is unable to employ counsel, and is incapable adequately of making his own defense because of ignorance, feeble-mindedness, illiteracy, or the like, it is the duty of the court, whether requested or not, to assign counsel for him as a necessary requisite of due process of law

carte.punch: Sentenced to death in a day, without a real lawyer: the Supreme Court says no in 1932
carte.idee: In 1931, seven young Black men accused of rape are tried in Alabama with a lawyer found that very morning. In 1932, in Powell v. Alabama, the Supreme Court says that, in a capital case, counsel must be appointed early enough for his help to count.
carte.source_courte: Powell v. Alabama, U.S. Supreme Court, 1932

quiz.question: What does the Supreme Court object to, in Powell v. Alabama, in the way the accused were defended?
choix: That a lawyer was appointed for them too late to really help them in a capital case
That Alabama law provided for no court-appointed lawyer, however serious the charges
That the Tennessee lawyer did not have the degree required to practice in the State
That the judge should have refused any lawyer, out of impartiality toward the accused
quiz.explication: Alabama already had a rule on counsel in capital cases; the Court holds that an appointment made on the morning of the trial, after the decisive preparation phase, does not meet the Fourteenth Amendment's due process requirement. It disputes neither the lawyers' credentials nor the judge's impartiality, and its formula is limited to capital cases.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what case does the Supreme Court say a court must appoint a lawyer even without a request?
choix: In any criminal case, as soon as the accused expressly asks the judge
In a capital case where the accused can afford the defender of his choice
In a capital case, when the accused cannot pay for a lawyer and cannot defend himself, through ignorance or illiteracy
In any case tried before a federal jury, whatever the seriousness of the charges
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court limits its requirement to capital cases, for an accused who can neither pay for a lawyer nor defend himself. It explicitly leaves aside other cases, which it does not decide.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens in the three trials, according to the entry?
choix: They last several weeks and end in partial acquittals for lack of evidence
They are suspended so the defense can gather new witnesses
They result in prison sentences, the juries ruling out the death penalty
Each is wrapped up in a single day, and the juries impose the death penalty on all those convicted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry reports that each of the three trials is wrapped up in a single day and that all those convicted receive the death penalty, which is the basis for the appeal to the federal Court.
